% v12 front matter and introduction. Every number is a generated macro from the v11 evidence build.
\newcommand{\vTwelveAbstract}{%
Review comments must follow revised code, and a relocated comment must not be mistaken for a settled concern. Review tools drop a changed line's position or move the comment without saying whether the reviewed code changed. We separate three properties that tools merge: whether the reviewed code changed, whether the anchor still points at it, and whether the supervisor's concern is resolved. We state five safety requirements over them, and a counterexample for each failure mechanism. A safety layer wraps any code locator: change labels computed from the reviewed quotation, indentation and copy guards on the returned window, and issue states that relocation cannot close. We tested it over a capstone review portal's matcher, the region mapper CodeMapper, a line tracker and two language models, on controlled edits, real and student-authored Python histories, a human-annotated benchmark, and \wkUnits{} GitHub review suggestions in five languages, whose application gives an annotator-free reference. CodeMapper located code better than the portal's matcher. Over CodeMapper the layer cut missed re-checks on real histories (syntax-tree reference) from \wiRealCmQMissK{} to \wiRealCmGiMissK{} of \wiRealCmQMissN{}, at the cost of confirmations on unchanged code. No locator showed a suggestion's target on wrong code without a request. Edits wrapping unchanged quoted lines evade every quotation check, a copy guard cannot tell identical copies apart, tuned thresholds did not transfer between projects, and the portal's lifecycle loses issues through deletion and dismissal; a model-checked contract closes these gaps. With no supervisor or student observed, the results show technical feasibility, not educational benefit.}

\begin{document}

\title{Living Review: Carrying Code Review Comments Safely Across Resubmissions}
\author{Raisa~Jose, Noel~Alex~Samuel, Khadheeja~Safar, and Kalyanaraman~P%
\thanks{The authors are with the School of Computer Science and Engineering, Vellore Institute of Technology, Vellore, India.}}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
\vTwelveAbstract
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
code review, annotation anchoring, source code tracking, software evolution, language models
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}
A review comment refers both to a location and to a concern. When code is revised, the location may move while the concern remains, or the concern may be addressed while most of the quoted code survives. In five open-source Python projects, \wpeOutdated{} of \wpeThreads{} inline review threads on merged pull requests (\wpeOutdatedPct\%; 95\% pull-request cluster interval \wpeOutdatedLo--\wpeOutdatedHi\%) were marked outdated by GitHub, and \wpeNullLinePct\% of the outdated threads had no position in the current diff, so the reviewer sees the comment but not where it now applies.

\sys{} is the resubmission model of a capstone review portal in which faculty supervisors review a team's code and report over several versions. Consider a supervisor who comments on version~1 that a retry loop in \texttt{client.py} never backs off. The team has an identical copy of the loop in \texttt{worker.py}. In version~2 it fixes the loop in \texttt{client.py} and leaves the copy alone. A quotation-based locator no longer finds the reviewed text in place, finds it unchanged in \texttt{worker.py} and reports the comment \lbl{moved}. The supervisor then sees the old comment on unchanged code, with nothing to say that the reviewed code changed, and may keep or close the concern without seeing the fix. This is the mechanism behind every missed re-check of the portal's deployed locator on real histories (Section~\ref{sec:layer}). GitHub would instead mark the thread outdated and drop its position. In the configuration evaluated here (the deployed portal still runs the cascade alone, Section~\ref{sec:impl}), \sys{} keeps the placement, but its copy guard notices that the quoted text was already in \texttt{worker.py} and asks for a re-check, shows the reviewed quotation beside the current code, and keeps the issue open until the supervisor decides.

The example separates three properties that tools usually merge: whether the reviewed code \emph{changed}, whether the anchor still points at it (\emph{validity}), and whether the supervisor's \emph{concern} is unresolved. The first two are properties of code and can be measured; the third is known only to the supervisor, and a change is evidence that a concern may be affected, not that it has been addressed. Whether carrying feedback forward helps supervisors re-review and students act on feedback is motivated by feedback-literacy research \cite{carless2018feedback,winstone2017supporting} but not answered by it. This paper addresses the technical problem and the issue-state rules that connect it to supervision; it measures no learning, re-review time or workload outcome.

Content-bearing anchors, fuzzy matching, diff-based tracking and region mapping are established \cite{brush2001robust,w3c2017annotation,asaduzzaman2013lhdiff,falleri2014fine,hu2026codemapper}, and review tools already port or outdate comments \cite{gerritporting,github2018outdating}. We claim no new matching principle, and the portal's own matcher is not the best available. The contribution is \emph{safety-aware feedback persistence}: a contract under which relocation evidence may move an issue only towards a supervisor's attention, stated as five requirements, and a \emph{safety layer} that applies it around any locator. Relocation results become change labels computed from the reviewed quotation, two guards inspect the returned window, the reviewed quotation is kept, and no relocation resolves an issue. The layer meets S1--S3 under stated assumptions; the implemented lifecycle does not yet meet S4 and S5, and we specify and model-check a contract that does (Section~\ref{sec:statecheck}). Because the layer reads only the window a locator returns, it can be placed over a stronger region mapper or a language model.

Outcomes are ordered by consequence. A wrongly placed issue misdirects a supervisor, whereas a missing location is visible and prompts a search, so the primary safety failures are \emph{missed re-checks}, changed or deleted code not returned to the supervisor, and \emph{silent misplacements}, an issue shown on wrong code without a request; \emph{misdirected} requests, \emph{lost} anchors and \emph{unnecessary re-checks} cost effort. Every recommended configuration is reported with these and its placement accuracy, six outcomes with their own denominators; acceptable rates are an institutional choice, so we report trade-offs rather than a pass mark.

\textbf{Research questions.} \textbf{RQ1} (location): how accurately do the deployed cascade, conventional review policies, a contextual line tracker, a region mapper and language models re-find anchored code on controlled edits, real Python histories, student-authored repositories, a human-annotated benchmark and applied review suggestions in five languages? \textbf{RQ2} (safety layer): how often does carry-forward fail to return changed code or misplace an issue silently, by which mechanism, does a locator-independent layer reduce these failures over every locator and at what cost, and which configuration should a deployment choose for projects it has not seen? \textbf{RQ3} (state contract): does the implemented lifecycle meet S4 and S5, and what does a contract that meets them require?

\textbf{Contributions.} (1)~A persistence contract: the three properties, five safety requirements with their assumptions, a counterexample for every failure mechanism found (Section~\ref{sec:props}), and a comparison with review tools and trackers on each requirement (Section~\ref{sec:related}). (2)~A safety layer that applies the contract around any locator, built into a deployed portal whose system of record is still the cascade alone; the guards and identity rule are evaluated, not yet deployed (Sections~\ref{sec:design}--\ref{sec:impl}). (3)~An evaluation on five populations graded by evidential strength, including an oracle built from applied review suggestions, with all six outcomes for every configuration, ablations of the guards, the identity floor and copy placement, simulated supervisor interventions, and configuration selection on held-out projects (Sections~\ref{sec:method}--\ref{sec:layer}). Its negative results: a language model's own judgment of change is not a safe signal, a provenance-based copy guard fails where a copy guard is needed, the guards flag wrong placements rather than correct them, and insertions around an unchanged quotation evade every locator. (4)~A check of the implemented lifecycle by static scan, bounded model and scenario tests, and a stronger contract that closes the gaps it found (Section~\ref{sec:statecheck}).

An extended technical report in the artifact gives every analysis summarized here.

% v12 Background and Related Work (condensed from v11 Section II).
\section{Background and Related Work}\label{sec:related}

\textbf{Robust annotation anchoring.} Work on annotation positioning after document edits \cite{brush2001robust}, robust intra-document locations \cite{phelps2000robust}, quote-based fuzzy anchoring \cite{csillag2013fuzzy} and the W3C text-quote and text-position selectors \cite{w3c2017annotation} anchors annotations by content. For code, Meta-Manager records edit provenance in the editor \cite{horvath2024metamanager}, and Magic Markup re-tags markup with a language model \cite{misback2024magic}. These follow one developer's working copy and its edit stream; \sys{} receives whole submitted versions and must decide, for each earlier concern, whether its supervisor needs to look again.

\textbf{Code review and warning tracking.} Modern review combines line-specific discussion with human judgment \cite{bacchelli2013expectations,sadowski2018modern}. GitHub marks a comment outdated when its diff hunk changes \cite{github2018outdating}; Gerrit ports unresolved comments to a calculated position, or to file level, and ported comments look like ordinary ones \cite{gerritporting}; GitLab can resolve outdated threads automatically \cite{gitlabautoresolve}, the opposite of human-only resolution. CodeReviewQA tests whether language models localize the change a comment asks for within one version \cite{lin2025codereviewqa}; \sys{} must find where reviewed code went in the next. Static-analysis trackers keep warning identity and review decisions across versions \cite{avgustinov2015tracking,li2024tracking,spacco2006tracking,sonarqube}, and ViolationTracker builds precise violation histories with introduced, fixed, deleted and reopened states \cite{yu2023violationtracker}. Its lifecycle is the closest model of a persistent issue, but a violation is \emph{fixed} when the analyzer stops reporting it; a supervisor's concern has no analyzer, so \sys{} never infers closure from a disappearance.

\textbf{Change versus concern.} Whether a revision touched the reviewed code and whether the concern about that code still holds are different questions: a fix may sit outside the quoted lines, and an edit inside them may leave the concern standing. A \sys{} change label answers only the first. We therefore use it only to ask the supervisor to look again and never to close or keep a concern, and Section~\ref{sec:suggest} tests a claim-relative question as an optional, non-resolving signal.

\textbf{Differencing and region mapping.} Line differencing underlies most revision tools \cite{myers1986ond}; our matcher uses Python's sequence matcher, an extension of Ratcliff--Obershelp \cite{ratcliff1988pattern,pythonsequence}. LHDiff tracks source lines by content and context \cite{asaduzzaman2013lhdiff}, other work tracks changed lines and program elements \cite{canfora2007identifying,kim2006program,reiss2008tracking}, ChangeDistiller and GumTree difference syntax trees \cite{fluri2007change,falleri2014fine}, refactoring-aware differencing adds multi-mappings \cite{alikhanifard2024astdiff}, and origin analysis handles renamed, merged and split entities \cite{godfrey2005using}. History trackers follow named methods, variables and blocks \cite{grund2021codeshovel,jodavi2022codetracker,hasan2024blocktracking,islam2025historyfinder}. CodeTracker's block tracking gives a block a structural identity through refactorings \cite{hasan2024blocktracking}, whereas a review anchor is an arbitrary line range with no identity of its own; it could serve as a locator under the layer for anchors that coincide with a block, but it is implemented for Java and is not run here. ReCite repairs kernel comments whose referenced function was renamed or removed \cite{sun2026recite}. Closest is CodeMapper, which maps an arbitrary region between commits by combining diff algorithms, movement detection and text search \cite{hu2026codemapper}. These methods answer \emph{where is this code now}; none defines what a reviewer should be told about the change, or what happens to a concern when the answer is uncertain.

\textbf{What is conventional and what is new.} Each element of the layer has a precedent: people resolve threads in GitHub and Gerrit, GitHub's outdating signals change conservatively, Gerrit ports positions, warning trackers keep identity and dismissals, and CodeMapper maps regions. Table~\ref{tab:related} scores the closest systems against S1--S5 (Section~\ref{sec:props}). None combines relocation with a request computed from the reviewed text, none marks a placement as ambiguous, and none treats a disappearance as a reason to ask rather than to close. The contribution is that conjunction as a locator-independent contract, and its measurement over five locators. Feedback research motivates specific, actionable comments \cite{hattie2007power,shute2008focus}, and programming-feedback tools support diagnosis more than planning corrections \cite{keuning2018systematic}; we know of no study showing that relocated annotations improve students' response to feedback.

% v12 Design: cascade, labels, safety layer, issue states.
\section{Design}\label{sec:design}

\input{generated/v11float-fig-cascade}

\subsection{Versions, Anchors and the Cascade}
A submission version $V_t$ contains files $(\pi,T)$ and extracted report text. A code anchor is $a=(\pi,s,e,c,q)$: path, first and last line of a span of height $k=e-s+1$, whole-file SHA-256 digest and quoted text. Let $\qbar$ be the nonblank quoted lines with surrounding whitespace removed. The quotation is matching evidence, not a unique identifier of a program entity. An issue may hold up to twelve anchors.

Relocation returns a new position and a label (Fig.~\ref{fig:cascade}). Tier~1 accepts an untouched file. Tier~2 searches $\qbar$ as a contiguous run of stripped non-blank lines in the same file and takes the occurrence nearest the old start. Tier~3 handles edits in place: it maps the old start through a line diff \cite{pythonsequence} of the previous and new file to an expected start $p$, scores every window of height $k$ starting within $p \pm r$, $r=\max(10,2k)$, by the similarity ratio $2\sum_i m_i/(|u|+|v|)$ of the joined stripped lines, where $m_i$ are the matching-block lengths, and accepts the best window if the ratio reaches $\theta$ (deployed default $0.85$). Tier~4 searches $\qbar$ in the other files in sorted path order. Tier~3 runs before tier~4 so that an edited block is recognized in place rather than matched to an identical copy elsewhere, and its window stays near the predicted line to avoid distant look-alikes.
\input{generated/v11float-tab-labels}

\subsection{Labels and Their Limits}
Table~\ref{tab:labels} defines the five labels; \lbl{changed} and \lbl{removed} return the issue for re-check. Normalization lets an anchor survive blank-line and formatting edits, but in Python it also hides indentation, which carries meaning: a statement dedented out of a conditional keeps its stripped text while its behavior changes. A \lbl{content-match} or \lbl{moved} label is therefore textual, not semantic, evidence. A second limit concerns copies. When the original is edited or deleted and an identical copy exists elsewhere, tiers 2 and 4 can return the copy as \lbl{moved}, which keeps the issue's state, so the change is not returned to the supervisor.

\subsection{The Safety Layer}\label{sec:guards}
The layer consists of the labels, two window guards, an identity rule and the issue states. The guards were derived from the failure analysis of Section~\ref{sec:layer} and evaluated under protocols whose text and code hashes were recorded before any held-out run; the deployed cascade remains the system of record.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Indentation guard (IG).} When a normalized run is accepted, the leading-whitespace widths of its non-blank lines are compared with the quotation's, relative to the first line and in absolute base indentation. For Python any difference turns the label into \lbl{changed}; for other languages only a relative difference does.
\item \textbf{Copy guard (AGi).} When a run is accepted anywhere other than the predicted start, the guard counts occurrences of $\qbar$ in the old and new versions of the candidate file. A genuine move introduces the text, so only an increased count yields a clean \lbl{moved}; otherwise the placement is kept but re-check is requested. The first version of this guard (AG) flagged every clean insertion directly above an anchor, because the pinned diff maps such an anchor's old start to the first inserted line; AGi also accepts the line to which the diff maps the anchor's own first line as the predicted start.
\item \textbf{Variable-height window (VW).} Tier~3 also scores windows of heights $k\pm d$, $d=\max(1,\lceil k/2\rceil)$, so that statements that grow or shrink are recovered with their new extent. VW belongs to the cascade's own search.
\item \textbf{Identity rule (ID).} When tier~3 accepts a \lbl{changed} window, carry-forward replaces the anchor's quotation with the matched text, so a wrong fuzzy match becomes the reference for every later version. ID keeps the quotation the supervisor reviewed, $q_0$, beside the current one, $q_t$. Relocation still tracks $q_t$, but every \lbl{changed} hop must reach similarity 0.5 to $q_0$, otherwise the anchor is reported removed, and the request is computed against $q_0$: an issue returns whenever the located code differs from what the supervisor reviewed.
\end{itemize}
IG and AGi need only the returned window and the two versions of the file, and ID only the quotations, so all three apply to the output of any locator. None proves identity: two copies introduced in the same revision defeat AGi, and IG is a layout signal, not an equivalence test. A provenance rule (AG2), which accepts a window by where its lines came from in the diff, is a negative result (Section~\ref{sec:layer}). Content alone cannot decide which of two identical copies is the reviewed one; it can only decide when to ask.

\input{generated/v11float-fig-states}

\subsection{Issue States}
When a new version arrives, active issues (\lbl{open}, \lbl{accepted} or \lbl{needs re-check}) are copied into its review with relocated anchors and a lineage reference. Any \lbl{changed} or \lbl{removed} anchor requests re-check; otherwise the previous state is kept. No relocation transition resolves an issue. A finding raised again by analysis is matched to a carried issue by category, title and overlapping evidence, so a carried concern is not duplicated. A new finding is also compared with the findings dismissed on the preceding version by category and the first 200 normalized characters of its description; a match is created already dismissed. That key is a heuristic: findings sharing an opening paragraph are conflated and rewording evades it (Section~\ref{sec:statecheck}). Notes attached to carried issues, including voice, video and image notes, follow their issue; notes pinned to code are re-found by the cascade. Fig.~\ref{fig:states} summarizes the lifecycle.

\subsection{Three Properties and Five Safety Requirements}\label{sec:props}
Let anchor $a$ of issue $i$ be reviewed with quotation $q_0$, and let $\rho_t(a)$ be its true location in version $V_t$, or $\bot$ if the reviewed code is gone. Three properties are kept apart. \emph{Change}: $\delta_t(a)$ holds if $\rho_t(a)=\bot$ or the code at $\rho_t(a)$ differs from $q_0$; edits around the span are outside $\delta$ (Section~\ref{sec:suggest}). \emph{Anchor validity}: the returned window $w_t(a)$ is valid if $w_t(a)=\rho_t(a)$. \emph{Concern}: $\kappa_t(i)$ holds while the supervisor's concern is unresolved. The first two concern code and can be scored against a reference; $\kappa$ is known only to the supervisor, and a change is evidence that the concern may be affected, not that it is. The layer computes a request $r_t(a)$ and the lifecycle a state $\sigma_t(i)$, and should satisfy:
\begin{itemize}
\item[\textbf{S1}] no unsignaled change: $\delta_t(a)\Rightarrow r_t(a)$;
\item[\textbf{S2}] no silent misdirection: $w_t(a)\notin\{\bot,\rho_t(a)\}\Rightarrow r_t(a)$;
\item[\textbf{S3}] visible absence: $w_t(a)=\bot\Rightarrow r_t(a)$;
\item[\textbf{S4}] human closing: every transition into \lbl{resolved} or \lbl{dismissed} is a supervisor action;
\item[\textbf{S5}] persistence: an active issue that no supervisor closes is active in $V_{t+1}$, and requests a check there if any of its anchors satisfies S1's premise.
\end{itemize}
Each carried anchor is thus \emph{verified} (placed, no request), \emph{ambiguous} (placed with a request; the copy guard has found the identical copies and could offer them as candidates) or \emph{missing} (not placed, with a request). Only a verified anchor is shown without a request. Where S1 and S2 hold, that is under A1--A3 and for changes inside the quoted span, a verified anchor is the reviewed code, unchanged; ``verified'' is this conditional implication, not a runtime certificate, and Table~\ref{tab:counter} lists where the assumptions fail. S3 holds by construction, because \lbl{removed} requests a check. S1 holds when the request is computed against $q_0$ and (A1) the window is valid or absent and (A2) normalization preserves meaning; S2 needs (A3) that a wrong window differs from $q_0$. S4 is a property of code paths and S5 of the lifecycle; both are checked in Section~\ref{sec:statecheck}. Table~\ref{tab:counter} lists every failure mechanism found, the assumption it breaks, a minimal counterexample and what remains after the layer.

% v12 System Architecture (condensed from v11 Section IV).
\section{System Architecture}\label{sec:impl}

\sys{} is not a separate service: the cascade, its labels and the issue states run inside the review composition of a capstone review portal used by faculty supervisors and student teams (deployment diagram in the extended report). Caddy serves the client and proxies a FastAPI application that owns authentication, authorization on every protected route, validation and all durable state. Celery workers on a Redis queue analyse submissions (rule checks, a language-model review and a partner claim-to-code tracer, whose results arrive as signed bundles) and compose reviews. PostgreSQL holds versions, issues, anchors, revisions and a change journal; archives and media notes are kept in a store addressed by SHA-256 digest.

\textbf{Data and composition.} Report versions form a chain, and each has one review document holding the supervisor's issues, each with a status, severity, category, title, body and up to twelve anchors. A carried issue's origin reference, \texttt{carry:v$t$:id}, records its lineage and makes composition idempotent; every edit appends an attributed revision and must name the revision it was based on, so concurrent edits are detected rather than lost. Composition locks the version's row, because several clients may compose it at once, and runs carry-forward before the new analysis, so that a finding raised again is matched to the issue the supervisor already has. The review page shows a banner (``$N$ points carried over $\cdot$ $M$ need a re-check''), a ``From version~$n$'' tag on each carried issue and a plain-language note on each anchor. An optional assistant edits review points only through journaled, undoable tool calls, and a resolve or dismiss it suggests takes effect only when a supervisor applies it. The evaluated functions come from a pinned source snapshot identified in the artifact; the guards and the identity rule were evaluated over that snapshot and are not yet part of the deployed composition.


% v12 Evaluation Method (condensed from v11 Sections V, VII-VIII method parts).
\section{Evaluation Method}\label{sec:method}

\subsection{Populations}
\textbf{Controlled edits.} Every Python file of 60--1,500 lines in the portal's backend and a partner team's tracer (\nFiles{} files, \nLines{} lines) was exported from fixed commits. A trial picks a 1--10-line anchor with a unique quotation and applies one of twelve edit operators (shift, re-indent, moves within and between files, duplication above, token edits, rewrites and deletions), each of which supplies the reference outcome; there are \nPerOp{} trials per operator and seed, on seeds \seedMain{} and \seedRep. They are text mutations, not necessarily valid programs.

\textbf{Real histories.} We formed pairs of consecutive commits and pairs ten commits apart in nine Python projects: four of our own (\rOwnCommits{} first-parent commits) and Requests, Flask, Click, HTTPX and Rich (\rOssCommits{} commits by \rOssAuthors{} contributor names). Anchors are statements of 1--10 lines in function bodies of files the later commit changed, drawn as a \emph{uniform} sample and an \emph{edit-targeted} sample overlapping a diff hunk; \rN{} observations from \rPairs{} commit pairs were retained. Source was parsed, never executed.

\textbf{Student-authored repositories.} As a stand-in for student code we selected \hTwoRepos{} public Python repositories describing themselves as capstone, senior-design or course projects, by a frozen search and screening protocol (team authorship, at least 2,000 lines and 60 first-parent commits), yielding \hTwoN{} observations (\hTwoTargetedN{} edit-targeted). They are student work but not supervised resubmissions, so they show technical feasibility on code students write, not educational effectiveness. No threshold was chosen on them; the corrected copy guard AGi was specified after the first copy guard's results on them had been read, so for AGi they are not held out.

\textbf{Human-annotated benchmark.} The public CodeMapper benchmark \cite{hu2026codemapper} provides \cExtHumN{} code regions whose later locations were annotated by people, in several languages, in two sets with manually (A) and automatically (B) chosen source regions (``Human A/B''), plus tool-derived histories (\cExtExtN{} regions in all). It is the only reference here whose labels people made independently of the authors; the suggestion oracle below uses externally authored data but our classifier. \sys{} sees each case as a file pair, so cross-file recovery is not exercised.

\textbf{Held-out stress seed.} Constructed indentation, duplicate-copy, short-anchor and compound-edit suites (\wiFrN{} cases) were generated after the safety-layer protocol was fixed. In the indentation suite every file parses and an edit counts as behavior-changing when the syntax tree of the enclosing scope changes; compound cells compose up to four operators. Their rates describe constructed cells, not prevalence. A parametric copy suite, generated under its own frozen protocol, crosses the number and distance of pre-existing copies with anchor height and the fate of the original (Section~\ref{sec:copysuite}).

\textbf{Applied review suggestions.} GitHub review suggestions in five languages give a reference that no annotator made: where the quoted lines and the proposed replacement occur at the pull request's last head decides whether the target was changed and where it is (Section~\ref{sec:suggest}).

\subsection{Reference for Real Histories}\label{sec:oracle}
Real-history references come from Python's abstract syntax tree. Functions are identified by qualified name and their body statements are aligned by normalized trees; equal statements give the new location, a statement in an equal-cardinality replacement is paired with the statement of the same type at the same offset, and a deleted target can be found as a unique equal tree elsewhere. Ambiguous cases are excluded for every method (\rExcludedPct\%). A recorded in-house audit of 40 decisions accepted 39; it is not blinded.

\input{generated/table-refaudit}

\emph{Blinded adjudication.}\label{sec:refaudit} Two hosted models, not people, re-decided \wrAllN{} stratified targets (plus \wrExclN{} excluded candidates) blind to the reference and to every method, from the old excerpt with the reviewed lines marked and the paired new file (Table~\ref{tab:refaudit}). They agreed with the reference on \wrPairBeamStatus\% and \wrPairNemoStatus\% of the targets decided by same-type pairing, the step that decides \refdirPaired{} of the \refdirChanged{} changed targets, and on \wrAlignedBeamStatus\% of the aligned controls. Agreement was lowest where the reference relocates code to another file, which the input does not show (on targets where the methods disagree, \wrDisBeamStatus\% and \wrDisNemoStatus\% overall but \wrDisWithinBeamStatus\% and \wrDisWithinNemoStatus\% of the \wrDisWithinN{} kept in the file), and where it reports a deletion: of the \wrDelWithinN{} deletions and relocations inside the paired file, both models contradicted the reference on \wrDelWithinSuspect{}, and on \wrDelWithinEdited{} of them they found the code edited rather than deleted. Both readings are changes, so this error moves placement, not missed re-checks. On the deployed cascade's \wrMissN{} misses the models agreed with the reference on \wrMissBeamStatus\% and \wrMissNemoStatus\%, and both contradicted it on \wrMissSuspect{}: on \wrMissLowering{} both called the code unchanged, which would lower the miss count, and on the other \wrMissOther{}, which the reference calls deleted, one model read the code as edited and the other as unchanged. No reading raises the count. Of the \wrExclN{} sampled exclusions, both models found \wrExclEdited{} edited and \wrExclDeleted{} deleted, so exclusion removes hard changed cases. Two models agreeing against the reference is evidence of a reference error, not proof; a blinded packet of 120 items is prepared for human annotation.

\emph{Direction of reference error.} The reference calls a target unchanged only when its quoted lines stand verbatim, ignoring whitespace, at the reference location; all \refdirCertified{} real-history targets it called unchanged pass this check. That shows the text there is unchanged, not that it is the reviewed code. All but \refcopyRelocated{} of these targets stay aligned or paired in their own function; those \refcopyRelocated{} left it and were placed on the unique equal statement elsewhere, and in the public histories \refcopySuspect{} of the \refcopyChecked{} checked landed where an identical statement already stood, so the reference may have taken a copy for the reviewed code; the deployed cascade requested no check on them. Counted as hidden misses, they raise the deployed miss rate from \refdirMissPct\% to \refcopyMissPctChecked\%, and with the \refcopyUnavailable{} unchecked relocations in our own projects to \refcopyMissPctWorst\%. Conversely, of the cascade's \wpaMissTotal{} misses \refdirMissAligned{} rest on an equal tree, \refdirMissPaired{} on pairing and \refdirMissDeleted{} on a deletion; if every pairing and deletion behind a miss were wrong the rate would fall to \refdirBoundPct\%. The bounds do not cover placement accuracy or unnecessary re-checks. The student repositories use the same reference.

\subsection{Locators}
Three conventional policies reimplement documented review behavior: \emph{fixed line} keeps the original span, \emph{diff drift} follows equal diff blocks, and \emph{exact quote} searches the same file for the nearest stripped quotation. \emph{Cascade v1}, an earlier internal version, searches other files before fuzzy matching, searches the whole file and uses $\theta=0.75$. The \emph{contextual tracker} is a pinned third-party implementation in the style of LHDiff \cite{oselvarlhdiff}, with its defaults; \emph{CodeMapper} \cite{hu2026codemapper} and GumTree \cite{falleri2014fine} are run from pinned releases. Two \emph{language models}, \wjModel{} (the model the deployed portal is configured with) and \wjNemoModel{}, act as locators at temperature~0: each receives the old region with 15 lines of context and the complete new version of the paired file, and returns where the region now is and whether it changed. Only public code was sent to the models. Any locator's window can pass through the cascade's quotation comparison (\emph{labels only}: \lbl{content-match} or \lbl{moved} when the normalized quotation is found unchanged, \lbl{changed} otherwise, \lbl{removed} on no match) and then through IG+AGi; the guards never move a window.

\subsection{Outcomes and Statistics}\label{sec:safety}
For a set of targets, let $C$ be those whose code was edited or is gone, $P$ the content-preserved ones, $S$ the surviving ones, $A$ all targets and $W\subseteq A$ those placed at a wrong location, and let $R=\{\lbl{changed},\lbl{removed}\}$ be the labels that request re-check. Then
\begin{align}
\text{missed re-check} &= |\{c\in C : \ell(c)\notin R\}|\,/\,|C|,\label{eq:missed}\\
\text{false re-check} &= |\{p\in P : \ell(p)\in R\}|\,/\,|P|,\\
\text{silent misplacement} &= |\{x\in W : \ell(x)\notin R\}|\,/\,|A|,
\end{align}
and the lost rate is the share of $S$ with no location. Tables abbreviate these as Miss, Extra and Silent, and add \emph{Misdir}, the share of all targets placed on wrong code \emph{with} a request; it includes deleted code relocated onto other code, which requests a re-check but points the supervisor at the wrong place. Placement (file and start line on surviving targets) and classification are scored separately, because a location can be right while its change status is wrong. The extended report lists every rate with its denominator. All safety outcomes are \emph{label} safety: whether a request fires when the quoted code changed, not whether the reviewed concern is affected.

Synthetic proportions use Wilson intervals \cite{wilson1927probable}. Real-history observations share commit pairs and projects, so we report fixed-seed cluster-bootstrap 95\% intervals over commit pairs or projects for headline rates and every paired difference, and state a direction only when the cluster interval excludes zero. Paired outcomes are also tested with the exact McNemar test on discordant pairs \cite{mcnemar1947note}. The \rN{} real-history rows contain 234 repeated targets across the two samples. Many secondary comparisons are reported without multiplicity adjustment and should be read as such.

\subsection{Protocols and the Strength of Each Result}
Every analysis added in this revision followed a written protocol whose text and code hashes were recorded with a timestamp before it ran, and every amendment before the outcomes it concerns; these are local records, not external preregistrations. A protocol that precedes an analysis need not precede exposure to its data: the re-aggregations, strata, identity-floor replay and policy selection read records whose outcomes had already been seen, and stay tier E1. A reproduction gate first required per-observation agreement with all \nTrialsAll{} archived controlled trials and all \smRealCasAccN{} real-history observations. Table~\ref{tab:evidence} assigns each result to one of five tiers of evidential strength, and the text names the tier of every claim. The language-model study registered its prompt, settings, populations and hypotheses before any evaluation call: \textbf{J1}, the layer lowers the model's missed re-checks, and \textbf{J2}, its silent misplacements, each judged by the paired cluster interval, with exact paired tests and Holm's adjustment as a secondary check.

% v12 RQ1: location.
\section{RQ1: Where Is the Anchored Code Now?}\label{sec:location}

\input{generated/v11float-tab-safety}

\textbf{Controlled edits.} The cascade reached a correct outcome on \casCorrect\% of the main seed's trials, deletions included (twelve operators of \nPerOp{} each) (95\% CI \casLo--\casHi), against \qeCorrect\% for exact quotes, \ddCorrect\% for diff drift and \lnCorrect\% for fixed lines; it placed \smCtlCasPlaceK{} of the \smCtlCasPlaceN{} surviving anchors correctly (\smCtlCasPlacePct\%, Table~\ref{tab:safety}, against \smCtlQuotePlacePct\%, \smCtlDriftPlacePct\% and \smCtlLinePlacePct\%); on the replication seed it reached \casRep\%. The conventional policies fail by giving up, losing every edited anchor and, for fixed lines, every shifted one. Cascade v1 reached \voneCorrect\%: it recovered slightly more cross-file moves but attached \voneWrongRewrite\% of rewritten and \voneWrongDeleteBlock\% of deleted anchors to look-alike code elsewhere, against \casWrongRewrite\% and \casWrongDeleteBlock\% for the final tier order. The contextual tracker is same-file in scope, so it loses every cross-file move; within files it was slightly more accurate than the cascade. The controlled mix weights twelve operators equally and is not an estimate for natural revisions.

\textbf{Real histories.} On the uniform samples most targets are untouched or shifted, and the cascade reached \rUCas\% pooled over nine projects. On the edit-targeted samples it reached \rOssTCas\% on the public and \rOwnTCas\% on our own projects, and Cascade v1, at its lower threshold, did better (\rTVone\% against \rTCas\% pooled). By reference class the cascade recovered every in-place and shifted target, \rClsMovedFileCas\% of cross-file moves and \rClsEditedCas\% of edited statements, whereas the three conventional policies recover no edited statement by construction. The contextual tracker placed more surviving targets than the cascade (\smRealTrkPlacePct\% against \smRealCasPlacePct\%; Table~\ref{tab:safety}), most of the difference on edited code.

\textbf{Threshold and design.} At the default $\theta=0.85$ the cascade relocated \thetaEditedEightyFive\% of edited real-history statements and reported \thetaGoneEightyFive\% of deleted ones as removed; at $\theta=0.50$ the figures were \thetaEditedFifty\% and \thetaGoneFifty\%. No threshold is best for both. In a factorial ablation over tier order, search scope and threshold, searching the whole file instead of the local window lowered the share of deletions reported removed by \wpaScopeGoneInt{} points on our projects and \wpaScopeGonePub{} on public ones, and running cross-file search before local fuzzy search raised missed re-checks by \wpaOrderMissInt{} and \wpaOrderMissPub{} points, so both deployed choices are supported on safety grounds. Leave-one-project-out calibration for accuracy selected $\theta=\wpaLopoTheta$ in all \wpaLopoFolds{} folds; the calibrated rows of Tables~\ref{tab:locator} and~\ref{tab:external} use this value. Its placement gain has a cost the miss and silent rates hide: with the guards at $\theta=\wpaLopoTheta$, \wiRealCalGiGoneKeptK{} of \wiRealCalGiGoneKeptN{} deleted real-history targets (deployed: \wiRealDepGoneKeptK{}) and \wiHumCalGiGoneKeptK{} of \wiHumCalGiGoneKeptN{} human-annotated ones (deployed: \wiHumDepGoneKeptK{}) were relocated onto other code, requesting a re-check at the wrong place (Misdir). Calibration for safety did not transfer: of \wpaConstrFeasible{} threshold choices that met limits on missed re-checks and on deleted code reported present in our own projects, \wpaConstrViolate{} violated at least one of their own limits on the public projects.

\input{generated/table-external}

\textbf{Human-annotated benchmark.} On regions annotated by people the deployed cascade found the correct line, or correctly reported the region gone, for \cExtHumDepAcc\% (placement on surviving regions \wiHumDepPlace\%), the contextual tracker for \cExtHumTrkAcc\% and CodeMapper for \cExtHumCmAcc\% (Table~\ref{tab:external}). CodeMapper recovered \cExtHumCmChars\% of the annotated character regions exactly, the cascade \cExtHumDepChars\%; outside Python the cascade reached \cExtHumNpDepAcc\% and CodeMapper \cExtHumNpCmAcc\%. Our runs of the pinned CodeMapper did not reproduce its published figures exactly (\cRepAObserved{} against \cRepAPublished{} exact regions of \cRepAN{} in the first set); we report our own runs.

\textbf{Student-authored repositories.} The deployed cascade reached a correct outcome on \hTwoDepAcc\% of the targets (commit-pair cluster interval \hTwoDepAccLo--\hTwoDepAccHi\%). The contextual tracker reached \hTwoTrkAcc\% when given Git's rename detection, as in the held-out run (deployed minus tracker \hTwoDiffLo{} to \hTwoDiffHi{} points), leading in \hTwoTrkLeadRepos{} of \hTwoRepos{} repositories, and \wiStuTrQAcc\% when given the original path only, as every locator in Table~\ref{tab:locator} is, the difference being its \wiStuTrRenamed{} placements on renamed files. On edit-targeted observations it leads under either rule (\hTwoTrkTgtAcc\% and \wiStuTgtTrQAcc\%, against \hTwoDepTgtAcc\%).

\textbf{Language models.} On the edit-targeted open-source rows \wjModel{} placed \wjPubSelfPlace\% of the surviving targets and \wjNemoModel{} \wjNemoPubSelfPlace\%, against \wjPubCmQPlace\% for CodeMapper and \wjPubDepPlace\% for the deployed cascade; on the student rows the figures were \wjStuSelfPlace\%, \wjNemoStuSelfPlace\%, \wjStuCmQPlace\% and \wjStuDepPlace\%. On the human-annotated regions CodeMapper placed more (\wjHumCmQPlace\%, against \wjHumSelfPlace\% and \wjNemoHumSelfPlace\%).

\textbf{Answer to RQ1.} At its deployed threshold the cascade is not a competitive locator: a contextual tracker, a dedicated region mapper and two general language models each re-find edited code more often, and its fixed-height windows recover region boundaries poorly. Calibrated and guarded, it is competitive on Python: it placed \wiStuCalGiPlace\% of the surviving student targets against \wiStuCmQPlace\% for CodeMapper and \wiStuTrQPlace\% for the tracker, and \wiRealCalGiPlace\% of the real-history targets against \wiRealCmQPlace\% for CodeMapper, but it then keeps more deleted code, and on the multi-language human-annotated regions CodeMapper still placed more (\wiHumCmQPlace\% against \wiHumCalGiPlace\%). The ranking of locators depends on the population and the threshold. A deployment should therefore be free to choose or replace the locator, which is safe only if the safety argument does not depend on it.

% v12 RQ2: the safety layer.
\section{RQ2: Does the Safety Layer Keep Changed Code in Front of the Supervisor?}\label{sec:layer}

\subsection{How Carry-Forward Fails}
On controlled edits and real histories no observation received a \lbl{content-match} label when the code inside its quoted span had changed, but on real histories \smRealCasMissK{} of \smRealCasMissN{} edited or gone targets (\smRealCasMissPct\%; Wilson interval \smRealCasMissLo--\smRealCasMissHi\%) were not returned for re-check, and \smRealCasSilentK{} of \smRealCasSilentN{} targets were placed on wrong code without a request. Every miss carries the \lbl{moved} label: tier~4 found the quotation in another file (\wpaMissCross{} cases) or tier~2 elsewhere in the same file (\wpaMissSame), while the original had been edited or deleted. The mechanism is a pre-existing identical copy; \wpaMissSingleLine{} of the \wpaMissTotal{} anchors are a single line. The cascade requested no unnecessary re-check on preserved real-history code; its cost is \smRealCasLostPct\% lost anchors.

\input{generated/table-stress}

The held-out stress suites show how large these failures become when their causes are common (Table~\ref{tab:stress}). With an identical copy near the original, the deployed cascade missed \wiFrDupDepMiss\% of the needed re-checks and silently misplaced \wiFrDupDepSilent\% of the targets, because tier~2 chooses the copy nearest the old start. All \wiFrIndDepMissK{} behavior-changing indentation edits kept their state under the deployed cascade, because normalization removes indentation; with IG+AGi+VW \wiFrIndCasGiMissK{} did, at the cost of requests on \wiFrIndCasGiFalse\% of the layout-only edits. One-line anchors missed \wiFrShortDepMiss\%.

The guards do not correct a wrong window; they flag it. Over CodeMapper the share of stress targets on wrong code was \wiFrCmQWrong\% with labels only and \wiFrCmGiWrong\% with IG+AGi, but its silent part fell from \wiFrCmQSilent\% to \wiFrCmGiSilent\% while wrong placements with a request (Misdir) rose from \wiFrCmQMisdir\% to \wiFrCmGiMisdir\%; over the deployed cascade silent misplacement fell from \wiFrDepSilent\% to \wiFrCasGiSilent\%. On real histories a misdirected request costs a short search. Counting the targets whose code survives, so that a distance is defined, all \wzRealDepMisN{} of the deployed cascade's misdirected requests pointed into the file holding the reviewed code, a median of \wzRealDepMisDist{} line from it. Only \wzRealDepSilSame\% of its \wzRealDepSilN{} silent misplacements of such targets were in that file, and the guards left \wzRealGiSilN{} of them.

\input{generated/table-locator}

\subsection{The Layer Over Other Locators}
Table~\ref{tab:locator} passes each locator's window through the labels alone and then through IG+AGi; the guards never move a window, so each locator keeps its placement (VW belongs to the cascade and changes placement only in its guarded rows). The labels alone already turn a window into a request decision: CodeMapper with labels only missed \wiRealCmQMissK{} of the \wiRealCmQMissN{} needed re-checks on real histories. The guards' increment is small on natural code and large where copies and indentation changes are common: over CodeMapper, IG+AGi cut missed re-checks from \wiRealCmQMissK{} to \wiRealCmGiMissK{} on real histories, from \wiStuCmQMissK{} to \wiStuCmGiMissK{} of \wiStuCmQMissN{} on the student repositories and from \wiHumCmQMissK{} to \wiHumCmGiMissK{} of \wiHumCmQMissN{} on the human-annotated regions, but from \wiFrCmQMiss\% to \wiFrCmGiMiss\% on the stress seed (paired cluster interval \wiFrCmGiVsCmQMissLo{} to \wiFrCmGiVsCmQMissHi{} points). The contextual tracker responded in the same way. IG supplies the indentation cases, which no locator reports (CodeMapper missed \wiFrIndCmQMiss\% of the behavior-changing ones, guarded \wiFrIndCmGiMiss\%), and AGi the windows that land on an identical copy. Tables~\ref{tab:external} and~\ref{tab:locator} differ in guard version (AG against AGi) and in metric (correct outcome against placement), not in data.

The corrected copy guard AGi and the first one, AG, give the same placements and differ only in which windows they flag. With IG, AGi asked for fewer unnecessary re-checks than AG over CodeMapper on every population (stress seed \wiFrCmGiFalse\% against \wiFrCmGFalse\%; student repositories \wiStuCmGiFalse\% against \wiStuCmGFalse\%), but it missed more where an identical copy sits just below the original, because the line diff then aligns the original's lines with the copy (duplicate suite \wiFrDupCmGiMiss\% against \wiFrDupCmGMiss\%; human-annotated regions \wiHumCmGiMissK{} against \wiHumCmGMissK{}). The registered hypothesis that AGi lowers unnecessary requests without losing safety thus held on the real and student histories and the held-out short-anchor and compound suites, not on the held-out seed as a whole or the human-annotated regions. The provenance rule AG2 removed still more requests but failed exactly where a copy guard is needed (duplicate suite: \wiFrDupCasAGtwoMiss\% missed, against \wiFrDupCasAGiMiss\% with AGi and \wiFrDupDepMiss\% with no guard), a negative result.

\subsection{A Language Model as the Locator}\label{sec:llm}
The portal already calls a language model, so we asked whether a model's own judgment of change can replace the layer. It cannot. Judging change itself, \wjModel{} left \wjPubSelfMissK{} of \wjPubSelfMissN{} needed re-checks unrequested on the open-source histories, \wjStuSelfMissK{} of \wjStuSelfMissN{} on the student repositories and \wjHumSelfMissK{} of \wjHumSelfMissN{} on the human-annotated regions, and placed \wjPubSelfSilentK{}, \wjStuSelfSilentK{} and \wjHumSelfSilentK{} targets on wrong code without a request. Comparing the quoted text at the model's window instead of trusting its answer closed most of that gap on the open-source rows (to \wjPubQMissK{} misses) and part of it on the student rows (to \wjStuQMissK{}), but not on the human-annotated regions (\wjHumQMissK{}), where only the guards helped; with IG+AGi the model left \wjPubGiMissK{}, \wjStuGiMissK{} and \wjHumGiMissK{} misses. J1 and J2 met the registered rule, a paired cluster interval excluding zero, on all three populations, but after Holm's adjustment over \wjHolmTests{} exact tests only the open-source pair stays below 0.05 (\wjPubJOneHolm{}, \wjPubJTwoHolm{}), so the small human-annotated result is consistent, not established.

The secondary model, \wjNemoModel{}, judged change more cautiously (\wjNemoPubSelfMissK{} open-source misses against \wjPubSelfMissK{}), and the layer again closed most of the remaining gap (\wjNemoPubGiMissK{}, \wjNemoStuGiMissK{} and \wjNemoHumGiMissK{} misses). Temperature~0 did not make \wjModel{} deterministic: a repeat of the human-annotated run gave the same placement, range and label for \wjRepSameAll{} of \wjRepN{} regions.
\input{generated/table-suggestion}

\subsection{An Independent Multi-Language Oracle}\label{sec:suggest}
The references above are made by us or, for the human-annotated regions, small. A GitHub review suggestion carries two anchors: the lines it quotes, $O$, and the replacement the reviewer proposes, $S$. Where they occur at the pull request's last head gives an oracle that needs no annotator: \emph{applied} ($S$ occurs once and $O$ no longer, so the concern was acted on and its code is at $S$), \emph{untouched} ($O$ once, $S$ absent), \emph{rewritten} (neither), \emph{deleted}, and \emph{ambiguous} (several occurrences). Under a registered protocol we took \wkUnits{} suggestions on source files from \wkPRs{} merged pull requests in \wkRepos{} repositories, two each in Python, TypeScript, Go, Rust and Java, chosen by star rank and licence: \wkClsApplied{} were applied, \wkClsUntouched{} untouched, \wkClsRewritten{} rewritten, \wkClsGone{} deleted and \wkClsAmbiguous{} ambiguous. Two independently written classifiers agreed on every suggestion. The scope is the file pair, so moves between files are not exercised (tier E4; CodeMapper also E5).

CodeMapper placed \wkCmQPlace\% of the applied or untouched targets correctly, the deployed cascade \wkDepPlace\% and GitHub \wkGhPlace\%, because GitHub gives up the position of every outdated thread (Table~\ref{tab:suggest}). GitHub's flag, read as it is now, also left \wkGhMiss\% of the changed targets marked current. Every missed re-check of the cascade and of CodeMapper, guarded or not, came from one mechanism that the earlier populations did not show (GitHub's flag, which follows the diff hunk rather than the quotation, also missed rewritten and applied suggestions): the suggestion was applied by adding lines around the reviewed lines, which stayed verbatim (\wkAppliedWrap{} of the \wkClsApplied{} applied suggestions, for example a new guard clause around an unchanged call). The change is real, but no comparison of the quoted text can see it, so S1 holds only for changes inside the quoted span. AG reduced CodeMapper's misses from \wkCmQMissK{} to \wkCmAgMissK{} at the price of more requests on untouched code (\wkCmQExtra\% to \wkCmAgExtra\%); AGi changed neither count of misses. No locator placed a target on wrong code silently; placement errors came with a request (Misdir \wkDepMisdir\% for the cascade and \wkCmQMisdir\% for CodeMapper).

The oracle also tests what a model should be asked. On \wkLlmN{} applied or untouched suggestions whose comment has at least four words, sampled per language and class, two hosted models were asked either whether the code changed in a way that could matter to a reviewer, the question of Section~\ref{sec:llm}, or whether the reviewer's concern was addressed, given the comment. Taking application as the reference for an addressed concern, the concern question reached precision \wkBeamClaimPrecision\% and \wkNemoClaimPrecision\% (Beam, Nemotron) and recall \wkBeamClaimRecall\% and \wkNemoClaimRecall\%, against \wkBeamDiffPrecision\% and \wkNemoDiffPrecision\% and \wkBeamDiffRecall\% and \wkNemoDiffRecall\% for the change question (exact McNemar $p$ \wkBeamMcNemarP{} for both models). It also recognized all \wkBeamWrapN{} sampled applications that wrap the quotation, which no locator signals. It still called \wkBeamClaimFP{} and \wkNemoClaimFP{} of the \wkLlmUntouched{} untouched suggestions addressed. On this sample, then, the concern question predicts whether a suggestion was applied better than the change question does; application is a proxy for an addressed concern, not a judgment of one, so the result supports showing such an assessment beside a request without showing that it helps supervisors. It may only order or annotate the queue, never resolve or keep an issue (S4).

\input{generated/table-copysuite}

\subsection{Copies by Number and Distance}\label{sec:copysuite}
A held-out parametric suite (tier E3) varies what a copy guard depends on. Its \wpNMain{} constructed trials cross 0, 1, 2, 4 or 8 pre-existing identical copies with the distance of the nearest one, anchors of 1--8 lines and the fate of the original; \wpNSame{} more trials let the revision itself add the copy (Table~\ref{tab:copysuite}). Without guards the deployed cascade missed \wpDepMiss\% of the changes, since any copy is found and reported \lbl{moved}. Distance decided the outcome and the number of copies did not: the guarded cascade missed \wpGiCOneMiss\% of changes with one copy and \wpGiCEightMiss\% with eight, and every miss of a guarded locator had a copy directly next to the original (\wpGiDAdjMiss\% of those changes for the cascade, \wpCmGiDAdjMiss\% for CodeMapper). An adjacent copy sits where the diff predicts the original, and the guards inspect only placements away from the predicted start. Over the cascade the guards turned misses into misdirected requests (Misdir \wpGiMisdir\%), not correct placements; CodeMapper placed every surviving original correctly.

AG and AGi missed the same pre-existing copies and differ in two conditions. AG requested a check on every original shifted by lines inserted directly above it (\wpAgFShiftExtra\%), AGi on none (\wpGiFShiftExtra\%). When the revision adds the copy, both are blind by construction, but AGi missed more: \wpGiSameMiss\% against \wpAgSameMiss\% over the cascade and \wpCmGiSameMiss\% against \wpCmAgSameMiss\% over CodeMapper (paired difference \wpSameDCmGiVCmAgMiss{} points, \wpSameDCmGiVCmAgMissLo{} to \wpSameDCmGiVCmAgMissHi). Grouped into issues of two to four anchors, fewer changes went unreturned (\wpCmGiIssueMiss\% of issues for CodeMapper+IG+AGi), because another anchor of the same issue often requested a check.

Anchor length acts in opposite directions on natural and constructed code. On real histories one-line anchors carried \wyRealOneDepMissK{} of the deployed cascade's \smRealCasMissK{} misses, and the guards left \wyRealOneGiMissK{} of them over the cascade and \wyRealOneCmGiMissK{} over CodeMapper. On the stress seed the guards' residual misses grew with length instead, from \wyFrOneCmGiMiss\% of changed one-line anchors to \wyFrTenCmGiMiss\% of anchors of ten or more lines over CodeMapper (cascade \wyFrOneGiMiss\% and \wyFrTenGiMiss\%). Split by the cascade's tier, its only confidence signal, and by whether a guard fired, every real-history miss of the guarded cascade came from an exact-match tier on which no guard fired (\wyRealQuietMiss), and of the \wyRealFiredN{} targets on which a guard fired \wyRealFiredChanged{} had changed and \wyRealFiredExtra{} were unnecessary requests.

\subsection{Ten Successive Commits}\label{sec:prefixes}
Errors can accumulate when an updated anchor is carried repeatedly. We replayed each ten-commit horizon of the real histories hop by hop and re-ran the reference from each chain's first commit to commits 1, 2, 3, 5 and 10; \bTwoChainEvery{} targets were decidable at every prefix and \bTwoDecidableTen{} at commit 10, the denominator of the endpoints. These intermediate references are the same heuristic, not independent identity labels, and the replay assumes no supervisor action. Endpoint accuracy of the deployed cascade fell from \bTwoSeqAccOne\% after one commit to \bTwoSeqAccTen\% after ten, mostly through lost anchors. Because a request persists in the issue's state, the relevant measure is cumulative: of the targets changed by commit 10, \bTwoSeqMissTen\% had never been returned. The last label alone is a poor guide, because a \lbl{changed} hop rewrites the stored quotation: it failed to signal \bTwoSeqMissLastTen\% of the changes since the original. In a Flask trace \cite{flaskchaincase}, the fuzzy tier moves a negative assertion's anchor onto a nearby positive one at hop~7, and later \lbl{content-match} labels certify only that the wrong code did not change again.

\input{generated/table-identity}

The identity rule closes this gap (Table~\ref{tab:identity}). With the default cascade it reduced the changes since review that the tenth label failed to signal from \wiChIOffMissLastTenK{} to \wiChIOffIdMissLastTenK{}, the number never returned at any hop, and the endpoints on wrong code under a final label requesting nothing from \wiChIOffSilentLastTenK{} to \wiChIOffIdSilentLastTenK{}. At the calibrated $\theta=\wpaLopoTheta$ the tenth label alone failed on \wiChICaliMissLastTenK{} changes, because the lower threshold accepts more fuzzy matches and each one rewrites the stored quotation; with the rule \wiChICaliIdMissLastTenK{} remained. For CodeMapper replayed hop by hop the rule cut wrong endpoints after ten commits from \wiChICmSeqWrongTen\% to \wiChICmSeqIdWrongTen\% and raised lost ones from \wiChICmSeqLostTen\% to \wiChICmSeqIdLostTen\%, so uncertain transitions became visible losses instead of silent drift; with IG+AGi no change since review went unreturned at any hop (\wiChICmSeqGiMissCumTenK{}, against \wiChICmSeqMissCumTenK{} with labels only). The floor of 0.5 was not tuned. Replaying every floor from 0.3 to 1.0 on the stored traces, unsignaled changes stayed at \wzDepMissRange{} for the deployed cascade and \wzGicMissRange{} for the calibrated one at every floor, because a request is computed against $q_0$ whether or not the anchor is kept; the floor only trades wrong endpoints for lost ones (at 1.0 the deployed cascade's \wzDepFFiveWrong{} wrong became \wzDepFTenWrong{} and its \wzDepFFiveLost{} lost \wzDepFTenLost). No floor separates the cases: on \lbl{changed} hops the similarity to $q_0$ had a median of \wzDepRatioTrueMed{} when the window was the true target and \wzDepRatioWrongMed{} when it was not. Recomputed on the same chains, CodeMapper returned different regions for identical inputs on \wiChIGateChains{} of 4,000 chains; all its rows in Table~\ref{tab:identity} come from one run.

\input{generated/table-interventions}

\textbf{Supervisor interventions.}\label{sec:interventions} The replay assumes that nobody acts on a request. A simulated supervisor acting at commits 1, 2, 3 and 5, and only on a request, may correct a wrong or lost anchor to the reference location, accept a correctly placed \lbl{changed} anchor as reviewed, do whichever fits, or dismiss the issue (Table~\ref{tab:interventions}); changes are counted since the last review. With no action the simulator reproduced the stored cascade traces exactly and CodeMapper's on \wvGateCmAgree{} of \wvGateCmHops{} hops, because CodeMapper is not fully deterministic. Correction repairs placement: for the deployed cascade it raised correct endpoints by \wvDepDPOneCorrectAbs{} of \wvChains{} (95\% interval \wvDepDPOneCorrectAbsLo--\wvDepDPOneCorrectAbsHi) with \wvDepPOneAct{} actions, mostly by recovering lost anchors, but removed only \wvDepDPOneWrongAbs{} of \wvDepPZeroWrong{} wrong endpoints, because most of its wrong placements raise no request. Acceptance cannot repair a label: without the identity rule it lowered missed changes by exactly the changes it had reviewed (\wvDepDPTwoMissAbs{} for the cascade, \wvCmDPTwoMissAbs{} for CodeMapper+IG+AGi). With the rule the accepted code becomes the reviewed quotation, so acceptance removed \wvDepIdDPTwoReqAbs{} and \wvCmIdDPTwoReqAbs{} later requests on code already seen, with missed changes unchanged at \wvDepIdPTwoMiss{} and \wvCmIdPTwoMiss. Dismissal at the first request ended \wvDismissedMin--\wvDismissedMax{} chains per configuration, and in \wvDismissedChangedMin--\wvDismissedChangedMax{} of them the code changed afterwards; a dismissal hides such changes by design.

\subsection{What the Layer Costs}\label{sec:costs}
The layer converts silent failures into requests, and the price is paid on preserved code: over CodeMapper, false re-checks rose from \wiStuCmQFalse\% to \wiStuCmGiFalse\% on the student repositories and from \wiFrCmQFalse\% to \wiFrCmGiFalse\% on the stress seed. Whether that pays depends on the share $p$ of carried issues on changed code, which no study here measured. With $w$ the cost of a missed re-check in unnecessary confirmations, $\Delta_m$ the fall in the missed rate and $\Delta_f$ the rise in the false rate, the guarded configuration costs no more than the unguarded one when $p \ge \Delta_f/(\Delta_f + w\,\Delta_m)$. For the cascade this break-even share is \wiRealBreakEvenOne\% on real histories, \wiStuBreakEvenOne\% on the student repositories and \wiHumBreakEvenOne\% on the human-annotated regions at $w=1$, and \wiRealBreakEvenTen\%, \wiStuBreakEvenTen\% and \wiHumBreakEvenTen\% at $w=10$; for CodeMapper, whose labels alone miss little, it is \wiRealCmBreakEvenOne\%, \wiStuCmBreakEvenOne\% and \wiHumCmBreakEvenOne\% at $w=1$ and \wiRealCmBreakEvenTen\%, \wiStuCmBreakEvenTen\% and \wiHumCmBreakEvenTen\% at $w=10$. These points ignore silent misplacements, which favors the unguarded configuration. The only external figure, \wpeOutdatedPct\% of open-source review threads outdated by GitHub, counts changes anywhere in a diff hunk \cite{github2018outdating}, so it is only a rough ceiling. On the human-annotated regions the cascade's break-even at $w=1$ lies above even that ceiling.

\subsection{Choosing a Configuration on Unseen Projects}\label{sec:policy}
A similarity threshold tuned on some projects did not transfer to others (Section~\ref{sec:location}), so we asked the question at the level of whole deployment policies. Every recorded locator and layer was a candidate; the policy with the lowest cost $C=w(\text{missed}+\text{silent})+m\,\text{misdirected}+\text{lost}+\text{unnecessary}$ per carried target on eight real-history projects was evaluated on the ninth, and likewise over the student repositories (post hoc, tier E1). Selection beat the deployed cascade on all \wzRealThreeFolds{} held-out projects at every weight and on \wzStuThreeBeatDep{} of \wzStuThreeFolds{} student repositories at $w=m=3$, but not a strong fixed default: against CodeMapper+IG+AGi it won on \wzRealThreeBeatCm{} of \wzRealThreeFolds{} projects at $w=m=3$ and \wzRealTenBeatCm{} at $w=10$, and the folds chose \wzRealThreeDistinct{} and \wzRealTenDistinct{} different policies. A course gains most by replacing a weak locator and keeping the layer.

\textbf{Answer to RQ2.} Missed re-checks are rare on real histories and come from identifiable mechanisms: identical copies next to the original or added by the same revision, hidden indentation changes, and, on applied suggestions, edits around an unchanged quotation, which no quotation check can see. The quotation labels remove most of a locator's misses on natural code; the guards reduce what remains on every locator tested and turn most silent copy and indentation failures into requests, but they do not fix placement. Neither model's own judgment of change was a safe signal; a question about the concern predicted applied suggestions better, a proxy that does not establish usefulness to supervisors. Keeping the reviewed quotation reduced the changes since review that went unsignaled across ten commits, to none over CodeMapper with the guards, with or without supervisor action, within the limits of the replayed reference. All of this costs confirmations on preserved code, and whether it pays depends on a share of changed issues that a course would have to measure.

% v12 RQ3: implemented state contract (condensed from v11 RQ6).
\section{RQ3: The Implemented State Contract}\label{sec:statecheck}
The safety argument rests on rules about who may change an issue's state. We checked them against the pinned application in three ways.

\textbf{Specification.} The extended report tabulates the implemented transitions (\wpdTransitionRows{} rows) with actor, source and target state and the source lines that implement each, checked when the table is generated; a last row records that no code path lets the system write \lbl{resolved}. Faculty status edits have no source-state guard: a supervisor may set any state from any state.

\textbf{Static scan and bounded model.} A scan of the abstract syntax trees found \wpdWriters{} call sites that create, update, delete, restore or undo a review issue, and no direct assignment to its status; none of the system writers writes \lbl{resolved}, so the headline property rests on the scan. A bounded model of the transitions for two findings and two versions, with every carried issue's relocation label chosen nondeterministically, visited \wpdStates{} states and \wpdTransitions{} transitions to depth \wpdDepth. No system event wrote \lbl{resolved} (\wpdSystemResolved{} violations), revision history stayed append-only, repeated composition changed nothing, and the assistant never closed an issue without a supervisor's confirmation. One invariant failed: an active issue was not carried to the next version on \wpdNotCarried{} transitions, all through deletion (\wpdNotCarriedFaculty{} by a supervisor, \wpdNotCarriedAgent{} by the assistant). Deletion is journaled and undoable, but a deleted issue is not carried forward, so the verified property is narrow: no system event resolves an issue, which does not mean that no concern leaves the workflow.

\textbf{Scenarios against the application.} Of the pinned application's own review-state and artifact tests, \wpdAppTestsPassed{} of \wpdAppTestsCollected{} passed, \wpdAppTestsFailed{} failed and \wpdAppTestsSkipped{} was skipped, none for reasons of review state. We then wrote \wpdScenarioRun{} scenarios that submit versions, import signed analysis bundles and compose reviews through the application's interfaces. Five claims held: a three-version chain was labeled moved, changed and removed in turn with its lineage kept; a change to one supporting anchor returned a multi-anchor issue; repeated composition was idempotent, and on PostgreSQL~\wpdPgVersion{} concurrent composers produced no duplicates; media notes followed their issue or code. Three did not, and the design text was corrected: dismissal memory compares only with the preceding version by a heuristic key, so a different finding with the same opening paragraph was suppressed and a finding absent for one version arrived \lbl{open}; carry-forward reads only the preceding version's review, so an uncomposed version blocks carry until it is composed; and an unchanged file above the carry size limit had its anchor labeled \lbl{removed}, a false re-check rather than a silent error.

\input{generated/table-contract}

\textbf{A stronger contract.} Table~\ref{tab:contract} lists each gap, the implemented behavior and a proposed rule. Its invariants refine S4 and S5: no system write of \lbl{resolved} (S4a) or \lbl{dismissed} (S4b), no assistant closing or withdrawal without a supervisor (S4c), and withdrawn issues visible later (S5-vis). A supervisor's withdrawal leaves a visible tombstone that later versions carry, and the assistant may only propose one; undo recomposes the versions composed after the withdrawal; dismissal identity combines category, normalized title and a digest of the reviewed quotations and is compared with every earlier version; a finding that matches a dismissal is created \lbl{open} with a note naming the dismissal, so the system never writes \lbl{dismissed}; and a version composed late recomposes its descendants. A bounded model over two findings with colliding keys, three versions and all sixteen label assignments of two anchors, covering every ordering of each gap's events to depth \wcDepth{} (\wcStatesImpl{} and \wcStatesStrong{} distinct states), reproduced every gap in the implemented contract, each with a minimal event trace, and found none in the proposed one. The proposed contract is specified and model-checked, not implemented.

\textbf{Answer to RQ3.} No system event resolves an issue, by construction of the code. The stronger property a course would want, S4 and S5 together, does not hold in the implementation: deletion by a supervisor or the assistant and an uncomposed version stop an issue from being carried, and dismissal memory creates a different finding already \lbl{dismissed}, a system closing. The proposed contract closes these gaps in the model; the portal still needs it.

% v12 Threats, Discussion, Ethics, Conclusion.
\section{Threats to Validity}\label{sec:threats}
\textbf{Construct.} Every reference here scores location and change, never the concern: a correct start line does not show that a comment still applies, and a \lbl{changed} label does not show that a concern is affected. The concern-relative annotation takes the application of a suggestion as its reference for an addressed concern, which a suggestion can satisfy without settling the concern. Sampled anchors need not resemble the spans supervisors select; supervisors may favor short, repeated lines, which the stress suites show to be harder. Edits around the quoted range can matter to a concern and evade every quotation check (Section~\ref{sec:suggest}).

\textbf{Reference.} The real-history reference is a syntax-tree procedure, not semantic ground truth, and it excludes \rExcludedPct\% of candidates, mostly changed ones, so its accuracies are conditional on a decidable subset. Its weak step, same-type pairing, agreed with two blinded models on nearly every sampled target, its errors bound the deployed miss rate between \refdirBoundPct\% and \refcopyMissPctWorst\%, the upper end coming from copies it may take for moved code; its deletions are its least reliable decisions (Section~\ref{sec:refaudit}). The adjudicators are models, not people, and the prepared human packet is unannotated. The two references not labeled by us, the human-annotated benchmark (\cExtHumN{} regions) and the suggestion oracle (\wkUnits{} targets, externally authored but classified by our code), score file pairs, so moves between files are exercised only on our own reference.

\textbf{Internal.} The guards were designed from real-history failures, so their real-history results are retrospective (tier E1); AGi was specified after an earlier copy guard's student and compound results had been read (E2); the stress seed, the copy suite and the suggestion oracle are held out (E3, E4). Policy selection, the stratified analyses and the wrap mechanism read records that already existed. Protocols are local, timestamped records, not external preregistrations. CodeMapper and the language models are not fully deterministic (E5).

\textbf{Statistical and external.} Observations share files, commit pairs and projects; with nine projects, project-level intervals are coarse, and many secondary comparisons are unadjusted. The histories are Python; the suggestion oracle adds Go, Java, Rust and TypeScript, but as file pairs at a pull request's last head, not as resubmission chains. None of the populations consists of supervised student resubmissions. The language-model results are dated observations of free hosted models.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}
\textbf{What was and was not shown.} The experiments show where anchored code is found, how its change is labeled and how often a request is withheld, on defined distributions; they are technical feasibility evidence. They do not show that supervisors re-review faster, revisit more of their earlier points or close fewer issues in error, or that students respond better. The direct test is a within-subjects study in which supervisors re-review the same revised submissions with a conventional interface and with \sys{}, measuring time to locate earlier comments, the share of earlier issues correctly revisited, erroneous closures and workload.

\textbf{Locator and layer.} Locating code is a matching problem on which stronger tools exist; deciding when a carried concern must be looked at again is a policy problem whose failures are properties of what a locator returns. That is why the same labels and guards lowered missed re-checks over every locator tested, and why the remaining failures (adjacent copies, copies added by the same revision, edits around an unchanged quotation, a deleted target placed on a look-alike) are the same for all of them. A model's concern judgment is a candidate annotation beside a request, untested with supervisors; no model output may close an issue.

\textbf{Configuring a deployment.} Four parts need no decision: resolution stays with the supervisor; requests are computed from the reviewed quotation, never from a locator's verdict; the reviewed quotation is kept beside the current one; and the strongest available locator is used, here CodeMapper. The copy guard is a choice: AGi avoids AG's requests on code shifted by insertions above it, while AG catches more copies added in the same revision that edits the original, so a course whose students copy and edit blocks together should prefer AG. Selecting thresholds or configurations per course from past data did not reliably beat a fixed CodeMapper+IG+AGi on held-out projects, and the identity floor trades wrong endpoints for lost ones without affecting missed changes. To make these choices from data, the portal should log, with consent, which carried issues a supervisor finds changed and which anchors a supervisor corrects.

\textbf{Ethics and data handling.} No student submission was used. The histories came from our projects and public repositories, the student-authored ones pseudonymized; source was parsed, never executed, and only public code was sent to hosted models. Portal telemetry requires opt-in consent that does not affect a student's access; a classroom study would need institutional approval.

\section{Conclusion}
Carrying review feedback safely is a different problem from relocating it. \sys{} keeps three properties apart, whether the reviewed code changed, whether the anchor still points at it and whether the concern is open, and states five requirements under which relocation evidence moves an issue only towards the supervisor; its layer applies the first three around any locator, under stated assumptions. The contribution is this contract and layer, not the matcher: CodeMapper locates code better than the portal's cascade on both references we did not label. Over every locator tested, the quotation labels and guards turned most hidden changes into requests at a measured cost in confirmations. What remains is specific: copies adjacent to the original or added by the same revision, edits that wrap an unchanged quotation, and requests that point at the wrong code. The implemented lifecycle never resolves an issue on its own but loses issues through deletion, dismissal keys and uncomposed versions; a stronger contract that closes these gaps is specified and model-checked, not yet implemented. The next steps are a consented study of supervisors on real resubmissions, human annotation of the prepared reference packet, and the stronger contract in the portal.
